title: Water potential
examples: How does the concentration of salt affect water movement into a cell?
Can you explain the difference between solute potential and pressure potential?
What determines the overall water potential of a solution?

explain.say: Today we are learning about water potential in solutions.

items: Water potential is a measure of water's energy.
It describes the tendency of water to move.
Water moves from high potential to low potential.

explain.say: The water potential symbol is written as psi. A lower psi means higher solute concentration.
Solute potential measures the effect of dissolved solutes on water potential. Higher solute concentration lowers the psi value.
Pressure potential is due to the physical pressure exerted by the cell contents. Turgor pressure increases the cell's internal pressure.
The total water potential is the sum of these three components. Remember psi equals ψs plus ψp plus ψg.
In a plant cell placed in pure water, water moves in by osmosis. This increases the cell's internal pressure until it reaches a balance.

draw.text: Water moves into cell by osmosis.

faq.q: What is the difference between solute potential and pressure potential?
faq.a: Solute potential relates to dissolved particles lowering the water potential. Pressure potential relates to the physical pushing force inside the cell.
asks: How does salt concentration affect the cell?
What causes the physical pressure in a cell?

faq.q: Does water always move to the area with the lowest water potential?
faq.a: Yes, water moves passively from an area of higher water potential to an area of lower water potential. This movement is called osmosis.
asks: Is water movement always downhill in energy?

faq.q: What is the role of the gravitational potential in water potential?
faq.a: Gravitational potential accounts for the effect of height on water potential. It is usually only significant over large vertical distances.
asks: Does height matter for water potential?
Is gravity part of the water potential equation?

faq.q: If a plant cell is placed in a very concentrated salt solution, what happens?
faq.a: Water will move out of the cell by osmosis because the external solution has a lower water potential. The cell will lose water and become plasmolyzed.
asks: Will the cell shrink in high salt?

faq.q: Can you give an example of water potential in action?
faq.a: A good example is root uptake. Roots absorb water from the soil because the soil water potential is higher than the root cell potential.
asks: How do plants get water from soil?
What drives water into the roots?

facts: Water potential is measured in units like megapascals or bars.
Pure water has the highest possible water potential, which is zero.
Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
The total water potential is the sum of three components: solute, pressure, and gravity.

quiz.say: A plant cell is placed in a solution with many dissolved salts. Water will move:
quiz.why: The external solution has a lower water potential, causing water to leave the cell.

wrong.1: This would only happen if the external solution had a higher water potential.
wrong.2: Movement always occurs across a semi-permeable membrane due to potential differences.
wrong.3: Water potential considers solute and pressure effects, not just height.

quiz.say: If a cell has high internal pressure, what term describes this potential?
quiz.why: Pressure potential specifically measures the physical pressure exerted by the cell contents.

wrong.0: Water potential is the overall measure, not just the pressure component.
wrong.1: Osmotic potential is a concept related to the gradient, but pressure potential is the specific term for physical pressure.
wrong.3: Solute potential relates to the concentration of dissolved particles, not physical pressure.
